entries.text: I notice e930198 and a9a97ab were synced before the segment fix went in, so e930198 still only shows the discussion-only T1/T2 turns. I should offer to re-sync with a force-push of the agent-ledger to fix this.

I opened PR #1, https://github.com/Oleks-Y/toolreader/pull/1, and linked it to this thread. CI passes. You can now see the agent's actions for each commit of this PR in the viewer, read from the `agent-ledger` branch, which is pushed too.

![PR commit ledger](~/.t3/userdata/browser-artifacts/browser-screenshot-127-0-0-1-muphjedn-430ae59b.png)

`#/ledger?repo=.&range=master..feat/commit-ledger` shows every commit with agent history (7 when the screenshot was taken; an 8th, the CI fix, has synced since). Each commit card holds its own turn → phase → action tree, shows whether it was matched by SHA or by commit time, and links the SHA to GitHub.

Running it on this PR's own history turned up three bugs, which I fixed with tests:
- **Two commits from one command:** when a single `git commit` command made two commits, only the first printed SHA was read, so the second commit was matched to the wrong action. Every printed SHA is now read.
- **Commands that only mention `git commit`:** text containing "git commit", such as a heredoc or a grep, counted as a commit and cut segments short. Now `git` has to be the command actually being run.
- **Discussion turns:** turns with no actions were included at the start of a segment. They're now dropped, and when a segment starts mid-turn, that turn's prompt is kept.

CI also failed once because the runner has no git identity. I gave the test repo its own identity and confirmed the test passes with an empty `HOME`.

Two <private> to know:
- The first two commits were synced before those fixes. So `e930198`, the top card in the screenshot, still opens with two discussion-only turns. Redoing it means rewinding `agent-ledger` and force-pushing it, which I didn't do without asking.
- Sync is still manual (`vp run ledger -- sync`, then `git push origin agent-ledger`). I haven't added a post-commit hook to run it automatically.

entries.text: This only reads the local agent-ledger branch, so in a fresh clone I'd need to fetch that branch explicitly from origin first.

The viewer reads the PR's commits and the local `agent-ledger` branch from a local clone of the repo.

**1. Get the PR's commits and the ledger into your clone**
```bash
cd .
gh pr checkout 1                              # or just be on the PR branch
git fetch origin agent-ledger:agent-ledger    # only needed in a clone that doesn't already have it
```
You can skip this in `.`, because both are already there.

**2. Start the viewer**, if it isn't already running:
```bash
vp run start        # http://127.0.0.1:4777
```

**3. Open the ledger page**
- Click "commit ledger" on the sessions page.
- Pick the repo path from the list, enter the PR's range (base..branch), and press **show**.
- Or go straight to the URL:
```
http://127.0.0.1:4777/#/ledger?repo=.&range=master..feat/commit-ledger
```
If you leave the range empty, it uses the default branch..HEAD, which is the PR you have checked out.

Each commit in the range is shown as a card with the agent's turns, phases and actions under it. Commits with no ledger entry show "no agent history".

**When there are new commits on the PR**, sync them and push the ledger:
```bash
vp run ledger -- sync --range <other>
git push origin agent-ledger
```
`sync` reads your local T3 and Codex sessions. So it has to run on the machine where the agent did the work. Anyone else only needs step 1 to fetch the result.

The page reads only the local `agent-ledger` branch, not `origin/agent-ledger`. If someone pushed new entries, fetch again before you look.

This is a sprawling request to untangle — polishing the project with more testing, using local Codex CLI sessions to verify display correctness, figuring out the most efficient way to store artifacts, deciding where CI/machine agent histories get stored, and whether this should run as a service, a hosted review environment, or just a repo tool, all while aiming for a production-ready solution.

I'm also weighing model choices for different roles — one model for threaded agent collaboration with auto classifier access, another for reviews, and separate threads for independent processes. On top of that there's the idea of preparing a website, which given the ambiguity I'm leaning toward interpreting as a landing/demo site — possibly a static build of the viewer itself reading ledger data straight from the repo, which would double as a working demo.

Given the scale, I think I should first check tool status, models, and existing usage to gather real context before designing anything. Rather than going through a heavy step-by-step brainstorming process, I'll do quick research, draft a design, and then ask a small number of sharp questions with recommended defaults attached, since the workload is large enough that going in the wrong direction would be costly, but full autonomy is likely what's wanted here.

My instinct is to recommend a repo-based tool over a hosted service: a CLI plus static viewer, with the ledger living in git rather than a server. CI agents would run their sessions, then a CI step syncs session logs into the ledger and pushes it — reading Codex rollout JSONL and Claude Code JSONL directly from files rather than going through the app-server, since CI environments have the tools installed anyway. Before committing to this, I want to check current status, available models, and what Codex sessions exist locally.

entries.text:
With my Claude session running low and Codex having more capacity left, I'm thinking through how to structure this larger effort - starting with a design doc covering storage, team integration, CI agents, and hosting decisions, leaning toward keeping an agent-ledger git branch for portability and GitHub visibility.

For writers, I'm considering local dev hooks plus GitHub Action steps for CI agents that read session files from Codex rollouts and Claude Code JSONL logs. For readers, I'm leaning toward a static viewer approach - no running service needed for PR reviews, just a GitHub Action building static pages published to Pages or as artifacts, while keeping the local server for live browsing.

Packaging-wise I'd publish as an npm package with a CLI binary supporting serve, ledger sync, export, and build-static commands, plus a landing page with a live demo. But the repo being private complicates GitHub Pages hosting, and more importantly, publishing session content publicly raises real security concerns since the ledger contains actual session data.

Given the scope and ambiguity here, I think it's worth pausing to ask about key decisions: hosting model, public vs private exposure, and which agent providers to support for CI. There's also the question of how parallel worker threads interact with git worktrees - since t3c starts threads in the project's checkout, concurrent edits could collide, so running sequentially or isolating to disjoint areas seems safer.

Checking whether t3c supports registering a separate git clone as its own project would let parallel threads work independently without branch-switching conflicts. I should move toward asking the user concise clarifying questions now, since my session budget is limited and I need to be efficient - starting with the delivery model question, where a repo tool combining an npm CLI with a GitHub Action for ledger sync and per-PR static viewers seems like the strongest recommendation.

That "website" question folds into whether it's a landing page plus demo or just viewer polish, so I'll fold that into question two. I've got enough clarity on the project now to go ahead and ask these questions.
Before I start several agent threads on this, three choices decide the architecture and what gets published. My recommendation is first in each.

Since there's no worktree creation available through t3c, parallel editing threads in toolreader would collide, so I need to either run them sequentially or have one thread edit toolreader while another works in a separate, unregistered project directory — though it's unclear whether pointing to an unregistered path would actually work. I'm starting to sketch out a sequence of steps to follow.

I'll write the design doc myself first, then dispatch work: an Opus thread with auto access for headless Codex reading and ledger sync, followed by review from a read-only GPT-6.1-sol thread. Given the scope, I'm breaking this into sequential threads — core headless functionality, then static site/packaging/GitHub Action, then testing/polish, then the website and demo — each reviewed before moving to the next, though I'm unsure if the testing/polish thread could run in parallel using a second clone outside the T3 project structure.

Rather than risk creating clutter by auto-provisioning a new T3 project, I'll keep <private> sequential and focus on branch strategy: stacking each piece as its own PR off the previous one (feat/headless-codex, feat/static-viewer, fix/display-polish, feat/site), all linked together. Before kicking off, I want to check the current branch state and pull ledger size numbers for the design doc.

entries.text:
Each commit's segment data is small enough to compress well in git, though I notice two commits share an identical segment, which is a minor dedup inefficiency not worth worrying about. With 2647 local codex rollouts available as test data, I'm now considering whether to write the design doc myself or delegate it to the first Opus thread.

I decide I should own the architecture. I'll draft a concise production.md on a new branch, keeping one concern per PR with the doc bundled into the first implementation PR, then write it on a headless-ledger branch based on commit-ledger so the other thread can continue from there. For storage, I'm settling on keeping the agent-ledger branch with raw JSON sized a few KB to tens of KB per commit, compressing well with git's delta/zlib, and adding an output cap (head and tail snippets marked as clipped) with a flag to disable outputs entirely, while leaving open whether this requires a format version bump. For writers, the first approach is a developer machine syncing from the local DB and Codex rollouts, either manually or via an installed pre-push hook that syncs the pushed commit range and pushes the agent-ledger branch alongside.

For CI agents, I'm working out running the ledger sync after the agent step using Codex rollouts scoped to the branch range, then pushing to the agent-ledger branch, which requires write permissions and matching commits made in CI by their SHAs. I also need to handle concurrent CI jobs racing to push the same branch — since ledger entries are separate files, a fetch-and-retry loop that recomputes the tree against the remote should merge trivially without real conflicts. Session matching in CI uses the workspace path to match rollout working directories, and for readers I'm sketching both a live local server extending the existing one and a static site generator for a given commit range.

For PR review, I'm thinking through a GitHub Action that builds the static ledger site for the PR's commit range and either deploys it to Pages or attaches it as an artifact with a PR comment linking to it — weighing Pages visibility restrictions on private repos against simpler alternatives like a downloadable artifact. Since fetching ledger.json via file:// won't work for a downloaded site, I'm leaning toward embedding the data directly inline in the HTML so it's a single self-contained file reviewers can just open.

Then I realize module scripts loaded from file:// are blocked by CORS in Chrome, so a truly single-file solution needs inline JS rather than relative asset paths — I'll leave the exact packaging choice open and let the thread settle it, defaulting to "open via file:// or serve via Pages."

For the npm package itself, I'm sketching a `toolreader` CLI (checking name availability, possibly scoped) with subcommands for serve, ledger sync/show/site/hook, and export, requiring Node 24 for native SQLite and TypeScript type support.

But then I remember Node's native type stripping doesn't apply to files inside node_modules, so publishing still needs a build step to bundle the CLI to plain JS — I should check how similar tools like t3code publish their CLI and copy that approach. I also need to plan a composite GitHub Action (`action.yml`) with inputs for mode, range, codex-home, and push, and figure out whether the website should live in a separate public repo given that GitHub Pages from a private repo requires a paid plan — worth checking the user's plan.

For the site itself, I'm thinking a landing page plus a demo built from a curated `toolreader-demo` repo showing real Codex sessions doing a small task, redacted and reviewed by hand. For testing and polish, I want a thread that runs the viewer against diverse real Codex CLI rollouts (exec, interactive, long sessions, MCP, patch apply, failures), compares the rendering to raw rollouts, and fixes bugs with tests using a preview tool in browser. I'm also working out the sequencing — polishing/testing should probably be its own thread based on master rather than stacked on the ledger branch, since it's independent work.

Given stacking is unavoidable to avoid conflicts, I'm laying out a chain: commit-ledger → polish → headless → static/action/package → site. I'm also weighing session limits — my Claude quota is nearly exhausted and resets soon, and I'm unsure if Opus threads share the same account quota, so I need to be mindful about how much parallel work I kick off. I'll write the design doc first before launching these threads with long background timeouts.



I'll draft the production design in docs/production.md, then have Opus 5.5 threads implement it sequentially on the shared checkout, with a GPT-6.1-Sol thread reviewing each step.

files.diff:
@@ -0,0 +1,44 @@
+# toolreader in production
+
+toolreader is a tool you add to a repo, not a service you run. The history lives in git on the
+`agent-ledger` branch, and every reader is either the local server or a static page built from
+that branch. Nothing has to stay up.
+
+## Who writes the ledger
+
+| Writer | Where its sessions are | How it syncs |
+| --- | --- | --- |
+| Developer with T3 Code | T3's SQLite DB, plus Codex via `codex app-server` | `toolreader ledger sync`, by hand or from the `pre-push` hook (`toolreader ledger hook install`) |
+| Developer with Codex CLI | `$CODEX_HOME/sessions/**/rollout-*.jsonl` | same; the rollout reader needs no T3 and no app-server |
+| CI agent (`codex exec` in GitHub Actions) | rollouts in the job's `CODEX_HOME` | the `ledger` action, after the agent step, with `--push` |
+
+- Sessions are tied to a repo by their working directory: a worktree of the repo, or `$GITHUB_WORKSPACE` in CI.
+- `pre-push` rather than `post-commit`: it runs once per push, sees the whole pushed range, and pushes `agent-ledger` along with the code.
+- `--push` fetches `agent-ledger`, rebuilds the ledger commit on top of the remote tip and retries on a non-fast-forward. Entries are separate files, so concurrent CI jobs never conflict.
+- CI needs `contents: write` to push the ledger branch.
+
+## Storage
+
+- One JSON file per agent commit. Today that is 6–55 KB raw, and git's zlib and deltas store about a quarter of that.
+- Outputs are clipped per action by default (head and tail, 8 KB total, marked as clipped); `--max-output 0` keeps them whole, and `--no-outputs` drops them.
+- Every free-text field is redacted before writing (`core/proof.ts`). It is a faithful record, not tamper-proof evidence.
+- Retention is git's: delete old `commits/*.json` on the ledger branch, or rebuild the branch.
+
+## Who reads it
+
+- **Local:** `toolreader serve` serves live T3 and Codex sessions, plus `#/ledger` for any repo on the machine.
+- **Static:** `toolreader ledger site --range base..head --out dir` writes a self-contained page: the viewer with the range's entries inlined. It opens from `file://`, a CI artifact, GitHub Pages or any static host.
+- **PR review:** the `ledger` action on `pull_request` builds that page for `base..head`, uploads it as an artifact and writes a job summary. With Pages enabled, it can publish to `pr/<number>/` and comment the link on the PR.
+
+Private repos: Pages sites are public except on GitHub Enterprise Cloud. Keep the artifact for private code.
+
+## Packaging
+
+- The npm package `toolreader` has one `toolreader` bin: `serve`, `ledger sync|show|site|hook`, `export`. The server is bundled with `vp pack`, as t3code does, because Node does not strip types under `node_modules`.
+- A composite GitHub Action in `action/` installs the package and runs `ledger sync` or `ledger site`.
+
+## Not built
+
+- A hosted team service (ingest API, DB, auth). Build it once teams need history across many repos in one place.
+- Claude Code and Cursor session readers.
+
